tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

T1.claim: Enthusiasts buy home espresso machines as a performance and status purchase, so a compact machine carrying commercial-grade components (as the Oscar line already does) can command a price premium over ordinary home machines.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who see the commercial components as a signal of quality and durability switch from mid-range appliances to a pro-derived machine, even at a higher price.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli keeps the price premium through its existing brand and shared component supply, without needing a new consumer distribution system.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not build a RATIONAL-branded home product now. Keep the professional business as the base case. If the home opportunity is pursued, the licensing or partner route (T2) is the lower-risk option to test first, not a RATIONAL-branded premium unit. Run the proposed concept test (X1) before any hardware or licence commitment. Note the Anova example weakens T2's claim that an incumbent brand is needed, so the partner question is open.

frame.objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks based on its combi-steamer technology, or keep focusing on professional kitchens. Identify what evidence would justify either choice, and separate what is known from what is assumed.
constraints: Outside analyst working only from public sources; no company contact or intentions assumed

alternatives: A. No expansion: stay with professional kitchens and the existing foodservice channel

C. Premium home line sold through premium kitchen retailers or appliance chains
D. License the steaming technology to an established home-appliance maker, earning royalties with no retail exposure
E. Professional-to-home bridge: a smaller or simplified model for serious home cooks, using the professional brand as credibility
F. Test first with low-cost signals (accessories, recipe or software offer to existing professional owners' households, or a direct-to-consumer pilot) before any hardware decision

T1.claim: Serious home cooks treat professional-grade equipment as a signal of skill and seriousness, so a RATIONAL-branded home unit can command a price premium over mainstream home ovens, and RATIONAL can capture that premium by controlling design, brand and specialist retail.
T1.who_benefits: Affluent, serious home cooks who want restaurant-quality results and status; RATIONAL, which would earn margin on a premium unit.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Buyers who already cook seriously and read about professional kitchens want equipment that visibly matches that standard. The professional brand supplies credibility that a generic home brand does not.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium hardware pricing, sold through premium kitchen retailers or direct online sales that keep the brand controlled. Margin depends on keeping the unit visibly 'professional' rather than cheapened.
assumptions: A meaningful group of home cooks will pay a large premium for a professional brand over a high-end home oven
Space, installation and power requirements are not decisive for this group
RATIONAL's brand carries recognition beyond the trade
Professional-brand cachet translates into home purchase intent
predictions: Stated willingness to pay for a home RATIONAL unit exceeds the price of premium home ovens by a clear margin among serious home cooks
Purchase intent is concentrated among existing enthusiasts and chefs rather than general households
Demand falls sharply once the price is set near the cost of a commercial unit installation
T1.first_claim: Serious home cooks treat professional-grade equipment as a signal of skill and seriousness, so a RATIONAL-branded home unit can command a price premium over mainstream home ovens, and RATIONAL can capture that premium by controlling design, brand and specialist retail.

T2.claim: Home cooks do not value a steamer's professional pedigree enough to pay for it; the home opportunity is open only to a licensing model, where an established home-appliance maker supplies distribution, manufacturing scale and retail shelf space, and RATIONAL earns royalties on the steaming technology.
T2.who_benefits: Mainstream home cooks, who get a steaming function at a mass-market price; an appliance maker with retail distribution; RATIONAL, which earns royalties without bearing retail or consumer-support risk.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Home buyers choose on price, footprint, ease and brand trust in appliances they already know. A recognised home brand, not a trade name, drives purchase at the shelf, so the technology has to be packaged by a partner that already owns that trust.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Per-unit royalty or licence fee paid by the partner. RATIONAL captures value without inventory, marketing or retail costs, but gives up most of the margin and control over the consumer experience.

The steaming technology can be licensed without damaging RATIONAL's professional brand
Royalty income would be meaningful relative to the cost of managing the licence

assessments.does_not_show: Does not show that home buyers are price-sensitive, that a licensing partner exists, or that RATIONAL would earn royalties. It records a general shift in the technology's category, not a RATIONAL decision or a home price band. The phrase about falling prices is not quantified in the source.

assessments.quote: These countertop appliances have the same characteristic changes as the full-size household appliances, except that they are smaller, and cost significantly less than a full-size oven.
assessments.does_not_show: Does not give prices, brands, or whether any home buyer pays a premium for a professional brand. It shows the countertop household segment is cheaper than full-size ovens, which weakens the premium assumption for that segment; it says nothing about the top of the market where T1 would sit, and it is an unquantified general statement.

assessments.quote: Subsequent products included the Anova Precision Cooker Nano and the Anova Precision Oven, a countertop combi oven that supported both steam and convection cooking methods and could be used either alongside other Precision Cooker products or by itself.
assessments.does_not_show: Does not show Anova's sales, prices, margins or consumer demand. It does not show that a licence to an incumbent appliance maker is unavailable or unattractive. It is one brand's product description from Wikipedia, US-focused, and says nothing about how the product is distributed or how much buyers pay.

X1.name: Brand-premium vs partner-mass concept test with serious home cooks
X1.method: Online concept test with a randomised two-arm design: the same countertop steaming function shown either as a RATIONAL-branded premium unit or as an unbranded or partner-branded mass-market unit at a lower price. Measure stated willingness to pay (Van Westendorp style), then a refundable pre-order deposit on a landing page for each arm. Proposed, not run.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 600 serious home cooks (cook at home at least 4 times a week, own a full-size oven) recruited via an online panel across Germany and one other EU market, roughly 300 per arm. Estimated panel cost and landing-page traffic within budget.
X1.measure: Primary: pre-order deposit conversion per arm. Secondary: median stated WTP and share of respondents above the premium-oven price band. Tertiary: stated purchase intent with space and installation constraints listed.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Branded premium arm converts at a meaningfully higher rate and shows WTP above the premium-oven band; the brand adds a premium that the unbranded arm does not capture.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Price drives conversion; the branded premium arm converts little more than the mass arm at equal function, and WTP for the brand sits close to the mass price. Brand premium is small or absent.

X1.decision_rule: Keep T1 only if the branded arm's pre-order conversion is at least 1.5 times the mass arm's and the branded arm's median WTP is above the premium full-size oven price band. If the brand premium is under 1.2 times, revise T1 toward T2 (licensing or partner route). Between 1.2 and 1.5, inconclusive; do not commit hardware spend.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE, not real data, not cited as evidence) is a what-if about installation coordination in a hypothetical group. It does not test brand premium, price band or licensing, so it does not change T2. T2 stays uncertain. The two real sources cited here are the ones that bear on T2: the countertop price point and the Anova consumer combi oven.

As a what-if only (SIMULATED, not real data, not cited in finish): if this offer test were real, it would show that installation friction lowers reservations for a professional-derived combi-steamer in a recruited home-cook group. That is a delivery and logistics barrier. It does not test whether a professional brand earns a price premium, so T1's core claim is untouched. T1 remains unlikely on the real evidence, which weakens its premium assumption without this result.

final.recommendation: Do not build a RATIONAL-branded home product now. Keep professional kitchens as the base case. If the home opportunity is pursued, test a partner or licensing route (T2) and a premium concept first. Neither route is yet supported. Run the proposed concept test (X1, about 14,000 EUR, 8 weeks, proposed and not run) before any hardware or licence commitment.
final.target_customer: Serious home cooks who already own a full-size oven, as the test population only. Not a commitment to any segment.
final.value_proposition: Undetermined: either a premium-branded countertop unit (T1), or a licensed steaming function sold through a partner's brand and distribution (T2). The evidence does not yet decide between them.
final.next_action: Run concept test X1 (branded premium vs mass-brand arms; pre-order conversion and willingness to pay). Keep T1 only if branded conversion is at least 1.5 times the mass arm and WTP is above the premium oven band. Also check whether RATIONAL already sells any household unit.
final.uncertainty: High. I did not establish that RATIONAL sells to individual buyers; its investor page lists only professional customers. Household evidence is general Wikipedia, not RATIONAL-specific. No financial data reconciled for a home line. Countertop units cost well below full-size ovens, weakening T1; the Anova example weakens T2's need for an incumbent. The 4.8 million potential customers figure is a company estimate for professional use. The SIMULATED result was not used as evidence.
would_change_if: Concept test shows branded conversion at least 1.5 times the mass arm (supports T1)
RATIONAL is found to already sell a household product with sales data
A home-appliance maker is willing to license the technology on acceptable terms (supports T2)
RATIONAL-specific financial data showing a margin case for a home line
Evidence the home market is too price-sensitive for a premium unit (further weakens T1)

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Do not launch a RATIONAL-branded direct-to-consumer home product now. The sources I read show RATIONAL as a professional and institutional supplier, with no evidence of its own household sales. Keep the professional focus as the default. If home demand is explored, test licensing or component supply to an incumbent home appliance maker (option E) and the installer channel before any consumer-branded launch. Run test X1 only if the licensing path is judged worth EUR 14,000 and eight weeks.

frame.objective: Decide whether RATIONAL AG should build a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or keep its focus on professional kitchens. Identify what public evidence would justify either choice, and whether a cheap test can separate the competing explanations of what home buyers would pay for.
constraints: Outside analyst using public sources only; no contact with the company and no knowledge of its intentions
Must first establish how far RATIONAL already sells to individual buyers, rather than assume it does not
Partly public financials: note what cannot be found or reconcile
Test budget of EUR 20,000 and a 12-week limit are analyst assumptions, not company figures
Search budget of 8 searches, 7 remaining
No SIMULATED results may be cited as evidence
alternatives: A. No expansion: stay with professional kitchens and the current channel only
B. Home-cook product derived from the commercial combi-steamer, sold through the existing channel (dealers and direct)
C. Home-cook product sold through consumer retail or appliance channels, with a simplified design
D. Serve the professional-adjacent segment first: small restaurants, caterers, and prosumer or enthusiast buyers, as a bridge
E. Licensing or partnering the core technology to an existing home appliance maker, keeping the commercial business unchanged
F. Serve home cooks indirectly by offering commercial-grade accessories, recipes or cooking content tied to the professional installed base

T1.claim: Home cooks would pay a premium for a compact combi-steamer if it carries the professional performance and reliability reputation of the commercial product, so RATIONAL could earn premium prices by making the brand the reason to buy.
T1.who_benefits: RATIONAL, through a higher-margin premium home product; affluent enthusiast home cooks who want restaurant-grade results
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Home cooks treat a combi-steamer as a status and results purchase. Professional credibility lowers their perceived risk and justifies a high price, as it does for other 'pro-grade' home appliances.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing and a brand halo on a product sold through RATIONAL's own or specialist channels, with margins above typical home appliances because the brand and technology are the differentiator.
assumptions: A meaningful group of home cooks has kitchen space and budget for a combi-steamer
The professional brand transfers to the home buyer's trust and willingness to pay
The technology can be shrunk and simplified without losing the perceived performance advantage
predictions: Stated willingness to pay for a branded compact unit exceeds the price of comparable premium home steamers by a clear margin in a survey of enthusiast cooks
Brand-known respondents score the RATIONAL-branded concept higher on purchase intent than the same concept unbranded
Conversion in a landing-page test is higher for the branded concept than for a generic one
T1.first_claim: Home cooks would pay a premium for a compact combi-steamer if it carries the professional performance and reliability reputation of the commercial product, so RATIONAL could earn premium prices by making the brand the reason to buy.

T2.claim: Home cooks do not buy built-in cooking appliances on their own merits. They buy them through kitchen-fitting cycles and retailer or installer gatekeeping, so a professional-brand product sold outside those channels would stall, and the value would sit with the appliance makers who already control kitchen installation.
T2.who_benefits: Established built-in appliance makers and kitchen installers, who control specification and the replacement cycle; RATIONAL only if it supplies them as a component or licensor
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A combi-steamer is a large, fixed built-in item bought during kitchen renovation. Buyers follow the kitchen designer's or installer's recommendation and the brand already in the kitchen plan, so the professional brand has little pull at the point of purchase.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Licensing or component supply to an incumbent home appliance maker, which captures the retail margin and the installation relationship. RATIONAL earns royalties or component revenue and avoids building a consumer channel.
assumptions: Built-in kitchen appliances are specified mainly through installers and kitchen designers
Consumers rarely switch brand from the one planned in the kitchen layout
Incumbent appliance makers already sell combi-steamers for home use, so an entrant needs their channel more than its own brand
predictions: Purchase intent for a RATIONAL-branded unit sold direct-to-consumer is clearly lower than for the same unit sold through a kitchen installer or designer
Enthusiast cooks who plan a kitchen report that the built-in brand is chosen before cooking appliances are considered
Licensing or supply interest from existing home appliance makers is more likely than consumer demand for a standalone brand
T2.first_claim: Home cooks do not buy built-in cooking appliances on their own merits. They buy them through kitchen-fitting cycles and retailer or installer gatekeeping, so a professional-brand product sold outside those channels would stall, and the value would sit with the appliance makers who already control kitchen installation.

assessments.quote: In addition to the professional food-service models, there are also smaller combi steamers for private household use.
assessments.does_not_show: Whether home buyers would pay a premium for a RATIONAL-branded unit, whether RATIONAL sells any household model, or how big the household demand is. It shows only that household combi-steamers exist, not that the professional brand transfers.

assessments.quote: Germany: RATIONAL AG , Gaggenau Hausgeräte , PALUX, Convotherm, MKN, ELOMA, Miele , AEG (part of Electrolux), Bosch.
assessments.does_not_show: Anything about how home buyers choose a built-in appliance, whether installers or designers gatekeep the choice, or whether the listed home brands sell combi-steamers to households. It supports only the narrow assumption that incumbent home appliance brands already appear in this product space, and the list is a general directory, not sales data.

assessments.quote: The customer base ranges from restaurants and hotels, company canteens, hospitals, schools, universities, the military, prisons and retirement homes to fast-food restaurants, party services, supermarkets, bakeries and snack bars, butchers, petrol stations and delivery services, including so-called ghost kitchens.
assessments.does_not_show: Whether RATIONAL sells any product to households, and it says nothing about how home buyers choose a built-in appliance or whether installers gatekeep that choice. The list is professional and institutional, which is consistent with T2 but does not test it. It is a company's own description of its customers, not sales data.

X1.name: Branded vs channel purchase-intent test for compact combi-steamer (proposed design)
X1.method: Online choice experiment with a crossed design. Respondents see a compact combi-steamer concept described either with the RATIONAL brand or unbranded, and either offered for direct-to-consumer purchase or recommended through a kitchen installer or designer. Measure stated purchase intent and a willingness-to-pay ladder. Concept text and price points are identical across cells. Proposed, not run.
X1.sample: Proposed: about 600 adults in Germany who report planning a kitchen renovation or new built-in cooking appliance within 24 months, with over-representation of self-described enthusiast cooks, about 75 per cell. Estimated panel cost, not a company figure.
X1.measure: Primary: purchase intent (top-2-box, 5-point scale) per cell. Secondary: share of respondents naming a cooking appliance as the first decision in a kitchen plan, and the brand uplift (branded minus unbranded) within the direct channel and within the installer channel.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Branded direct-to-consumer intent is high and the brand uplift in the direct channel is large (15 percentage points or more). Brand uplift is similar in the installer channel. Respondents accept a premium price over comparable home steamers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Direct-to-consumer intent is low for both branded and unbranded concepts. Installer-channel intent is clearly higher than direct. Brand uplift within the direct channel is small (under 5 points). Respondents say the kitchen plan or installer decides the brand first.

X1.decision_rule: Favour T1 if branded direct-to-consumer intent is at least 20% top-2-box and the direct-channel brand uplift is at least 15 points. Favour T2 if installer-channel intent exceeds direct-channel intent by at least 10 points and direct-channel brand uplift is under 5 points. If neither holds, neither theory is supported and the test is inconclusive; do not pursue a consumer launch. Thresholds are proposed analyst judgements, not measured values.

revisions.reason: I read the SIMULATED result as a what-if and excluded it from my evidence. Even if real, it bears only weakly on T2. It compares installation-coordination offers within one recruited group, not brand or channel control at purchase. It suggests extra intermediary steps reduce uptake, which does not show installers or designers gatekeep the brand choice, T2's core claim. T2 remains untested on its central mechanism.

The SIMULATED result is excluded from evidence. It tests installation coordination, not brand premium, so it does not bear on T1's claim that a professional brand earns a premium. T1 remains untested. The only real evidence is that household combi-steamers exist, which is neutral for T1.

Hypothetical only, as the stage asks: if SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE were real, it would compare installation-coordination offers within one recruited group, not brand or channel control at purchase. It would suggest extra intermediary steps reduce uptake, which does not show installers or designers gatekeep brand choice. T2 stays untested on its core mechanism. Not used as evidence in the finish.

final.recommendation: Do not launch a RATIONAL-branded direct-to-consumer home product now. Keep the professional and institutional focus as the default. If home demand is explored, first test licensing or component supply to an incumbent home appliance maker, and the installer channel, before any consumer-branded launch. Run test X1 only if the licensing path is judged worth an estimated EUR 14,000 and eight weeks. This is a proposed test, not a result.
final.target_customer: No home-cook target is recommended yet. If one is pursued later, the candidates are enthusiast home cooks with a planned kitchen renovation, reached through installers or designers, not through RATIONAL's own channel.
final.value_proposition: Not yet established. The only candidate is a licensed or component-supplied professional technology whose brand value depends on untested home-buyer willingness to pay.
final.next_action: Before any test, check directly whether RATIONAL sells any household product, since my sources did not show it. Then decide whether the licensing path is worth exploring. Only then consider running X1 (about 600 respondents, estimated EUR 14,000, eight weeks).
final.uncertainty: Large. The sources describe RATIONAL as a professional supplier and note that household combi-steamers exist from other makers, but none show RATIONAL's own household sales, household demand size, or willingness to pay for a branded unit. The 2024 figures (sales EUR 1,194m, EBIT EUR 314m, 26% margin, 50% global share) are company claims I could not reconcile with independent sources. Test costs and thresholds are my estimates. No evidence I read directly tests T2's gatekeeping mechanism.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers.
